questions.author: owner
questions.question: When was it known for sure that no strategy beat plain HODL, and why was the project continued if it turned out the strategies did not work?
questions.reference: On the evening of 26.08 the abandonment threshold set that day was formally met: the hedged and flat-only families showed no edge over their benchmarks, rotation was the worst of all, and the production v1.1 ended below its starting $5k on mainnet and Arbitrum, its active management costing more than it gave. The premise is not quite right: a wide passive LP of ±50% ('HODL with yield') beat HODL over the full period on 4 of 4 pools, as an allocation product rather than an algorithm. The project went on because the owner, after a discussion of the literature (about half of LPs lose to HODL, so the results match the market; full range does best, as the ±50% did), chose one final round instead of freezing at once, under a fixed rule: product or freeze after it, no further experiments.

facts.a: 26.08 evening: the abandonment threshold was met (hedged and flat-only families without an edge; v1.1 below its starting $5k on mainnet/Arbitrum; active management cost more than it gave)
facts.b: one result survived: wide passive LP ±50% beat HODL over the full period on 4/4 pools (an allocation product, not an algorithm)
facts.c: the owner chose one final round instead of an immediate freeze, after the literature showed about half of LPs lose to HODL (results consistent with the market)
facts.d: fixed rule: after that round, product or freeze, no further experiments

questions.author: owner
questions.question: Could the simulation of the algorithms have made a calculation error, so that some strategy actually did beat HODL?
questions.reference: The corpus does not prove the simulator right, but it records how its results were checked and which errors were found: the validation itself caught an engine bug (probe swaps through empty ticks faked trend signals and made exit variants show -100%; filtered on 17.08, baselines unaffected, verdict unchanged); the final round was recomputed independently on 8 of 8 walk-forward files and agreed with CC-Win's reports to the hundredth; a nightly report that called FlatOnly 'better than HODL' when it was only 'positive' was corrected against its own numbers; a corrupted first price point in a 720-day cache was flagged. After the volatility measure was corrected, the recalibration series still passed zero gates, and the overall result matches the literature (about half of LPs lose to HODL). One strategy did beat HODL over the full period, the wide passive ±50%, so the claim concerns the active strategies.
